hook.text: Marine heat waves are like heat waves on land — but underwater and they can last for months.

buildup.text: Persistent patches of ocean warm far above normal, stressing every living thing within them.

discovery.text: The 'Blob' — a marine heat wave in the Pacific from 2013 to 2016 — killed millions of seabirds.

twist.text: Marine heat waves have doubled in frequency since the 1980s and are getting longer.

climax.text: They trigger mass bleaching, kelp die-offs, and fish migration — reshaping ocean ecosystems.

punchline.text: The ocean can run a fever. And fevers are getting more frequent.

quiz.question: How have marine heat waves changed since the 1980s?

details.summary: Marine heat waves are prolonged periods of abnormally high ocean temperatures that can last weeks to months. They bleach coral, kill fish, displace species, and disrupt fisheries. Their frequency has doubled since the 1980s due to human-caused warming.
details.whyItMatters: Marine heat waves cause sudden ecological and economic damage. As they become more frequent and intense, coastal communities face growing threats to food and livelihoods.
takeaways: Marine heat waves have doubled in frequency since the 1980s
They trigger coral bleaching and mass fish die-offs
Events can persist for weeks to months across vast areas

faq.question: What defines a marine heat wave?
faq.answer: A marine heat wave is defined as a period of at least five consecutive days where sea surface temperatures exceed the 90th percentile of the historical average for that location and time of year.

faq.question: What was the most destructive marine heat wave?
faq.answer: The northeast Pacific 'Blob' from 2013 to 2016 warmed a vast stretch of ocean by up to 3 degrees C. It caused massive seabird die-offs, harmful algal blooms, collapsed fisheries, and contributed to severe drought in western North America.
